claim: A well-characterized metabolic landmark for aggressive cancers is the reprogramming from oxidative phosphorylation to aerobic glycolysis, referred to as the Warburg effect.
source: A well-characterized metabolic landmark for aggressive cancers is the reprogramming from oxidative phosphorylation to aerobic glycolysis, referred to as the Warburg effect.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about cancer metabolism, widely recognized in the field.

claim: Activation of the oncogene PDGF/VEGF-receptor (Pvr) in the Drosophila wing imaginal disc induces a glycolytic tumor.
source: In order to establish a system where individual components of oncogenic signals and metabolic pathways can be readily elucidated, we induced a glycolytic tumor in the Drosophila wing imaginal disc by activating the oncogene PDGF/VEGF-receptor (Pvr).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Pvr activation causes activation of multiple oncogenic pathways including Ras, PI3K/Akt, Raf/ERK, Src and JNK.
source: This causes activation of multiple oncogenic pathways including Ras, PI3K/Akt, Raf/ERK, Src and JNK.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing phosphorylation of pathway components in Pvr-activated tissues.

claim: The network of genes activated by Pvr stabilizes Hifα (Sima).
source: Together this network of genes stabilizes Hifα (Sima) that in turn, transcriptionally up-regulates many genes encoding glycolytic enzymes.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing Sima protein accumulation in Pvr-activated tissues.

claim: Hifα (Sima) transcriptionally up-regulates many genes encoding glycolytic enzymes.
source: Together this network of genes stabilizes Hifα (Sima) that in turn, transcriptionally up-regulates many genes encoding glycolytic enzymes.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing upregulation of glycolytic enzyme transcripts in a Sima-dependent manner.

claim: The network of genes activated by Pvr causes inhibition of pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) activity resulting in diminished ox-phos levels.
source: Collectively, this network of genes also causes inhibition of pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) activity resulting in diminished ox-phos levels.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing phosphorylated (inactive) PDH in Pvr-activated tissues.

claim: High ROS produced during metabolic reprogramming functions as a feedback signal to consolidate this metabolic reprogramming.
source: The high ROS produced during this process functions as a feedback signal to consolidate this metabolic reprogramming.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that ROS scavenging suppresses metabolic reprogramming markers.

claim: Warburg discovered that many cancer cells reprogram their glucose metabolism by transitioning from oxidative phosphorylation to glycolysis even in the presence of oxygen.
source: Warburg discovered that many cancer cells reprogram their glucose metabolism by transitioning from oxidative phosphorylation to glycolysis even in the presence of oxygen (Warburg, 1956a, 1956b; Vander Heiden et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citations to Warburg's original work and review articles.

claim: The ability of cancer cells to acquire aerobic glycolysis has been referred to as the 'Warburg effect'.
source: Such a metabolic state was termed 'aerobic glycolysis' and the ability of cancer cells to acquire this new metabolic state has since been referred to as the 'Warburg effect'.
evidence: This is established terminology in cancer metabolism research.

claim: Altered metabolism is an important element that contributes to the etiology of cancer.
source: However, more recent studies have explored the link between metabolic processes and oncogenesis, and have noted that altered metabolism is an important element that contributes to the etiology of cancer (Pavlova and Thompson, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article summarizing current understanding in the field.

claim: Drugs targeting key regulators of aerobic glycolysis are being developed to be included in the cancer therapy regimen.
source: Drugs targeting key regulators of aerobic glycolysis are being developed to be included in the cancer therapy regimen (Weinberg and Chandel, 2015; Galluzzi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to articles discussing therapeutic approaches.

claim: Several oncogenic pathways, including PI3K/TOR, JNK, Ras/ERK, regulate the catalytic activity or expression of key metabolic enzymes.
source: Several oncogenic pathways, including PI3K/TOR, JNK, Ras/ERK, regulate the catalytic activity or expression of key metabolic enzymes (Chambers and LoGrasso, 2011; Jones and Thompson, 2009; DeBerardinis et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on oncogenic pathway regulation of metabolism.

claim: Pyruvate is the key metabolite that is used to control the last step of glycolysis in a tumor.
source: Pyruvate is the key metabolite that is used to control the last step of glycolysis in a tumor, and in the presence of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), pyruvate is converted to lactate.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about glycolysis.

claim: In the presence of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), pyruvate is converted to lactate.
source: Pyruvate is the key metabolite that is used to control the last step of glycolysis in a tumor, and in the presence of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), pyruvate is converted to lactate.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about the function of LDH.

claim: Oxidative phosphorylation requires the mitochondrial enzyme complex pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) that converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, essential for the initiation of the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle.
source: In contrast, oxidative phosphorylation requires the mitochondrial enzyme complex pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) that converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, essential for the initiation of the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle (Linn et al., 1969; Leiter et al., 1978).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge supported by citations to foundational research.

claim: PDH is rendered inactive when it is phosphorylated by pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDHK).
source: PDH is rendered inactive when it is phosphorylated by pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDHK) and is activated when dephosphorylated by the phosphatase, PDHP (Harris et al., 2002; Bowker-Kinley et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PDH is activated when dephosphorylated by the phosphatase, PDHP.
source: PDH is rendered inactive when it is phosphorylated by pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDHK) and is activated when dephosphorylated by the phosphatase, PDHP (Harris et al., 2002; Bowker-Kinley et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Many cancers maintain high ox-phos as well as glycolysis, maximizing the anapleuretic functions of the cell that provide the building blocks for lipid, protein and nucleotide synthesis.
source: Many cancers maintain high ox-phos as well as glycolysis, maximizing the anapleuretic functions of the cell that provide the building blocks for lipid, protein and nucleotide synthesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cancer metabolism.

claim: The mammalian transcription factor, Hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (Hif-1α; called Sima or Hifα in Drosophila), regulates a number of target genes that promote various aspects of cancer, including metabolism, angiogenesis, cell survival, drug resistance, and invasive motility.
source: The mammalian transcription factor, Hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (Hif-1α; called Sima or Hifα in Drosophila), regulates a number of target genes that promote various aspects of cancer, including metabolism, angiogenesis, cell survival, drug resistance, and invasive motility (Wykoff et al., 2000; Carmeliet et al., 1998; Ryan et al., 1998; Pennacchietti et al., 2003; Ema et al., 1997; Semenza, 2003; Dang and Semenza, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published research on Hif-1α function.

claim: Hif-1α participates in metabolic reprogramming as hypoxia favors glycolysis over oxidative phosphorylation for ATP generation.
source: Hif-1α participates in this process as hypoxia favors glycolysis over oxidative phosphorylation for ATP generation (Zhong et al., 2000; Keith and Simon, 2007; Bertout et al., 2008; Dang and Semenza, 1999; Kim et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on Hif-1α and hypoxia.

claim: Hypoxia has been the proposed mechanism for oncogenes to effect a change in metabolic state.
source: Hypoxia has been the proposed mechanism for oncogenes to effect a change in metabolic state (Finley et al., 2013; Ying et al., 2012; Vander Heiden et al., 2009; Levine and Puzio-Kuter, 2010; Fukuda et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research proposing hypoxia as a mechanism.

claim: Mammalian studies often involve immortalized cell-lines with a variable and often unknown genetic background.
source: Mammalian studies often involve immortalized cell-lines with a variable and often unknown genetic background.
evidence: This is a general observation about the limitations of mammalian cell line studies.

claim: The mechanism for the maintenance of the altered metabolic state under normoxic conditions is not as clear.
source: Furthermore, while initiation of glycolysis has been studied (Lunt and Vander Heiden, 2011), the mechanism for the maintenance of the altered metabolic state under normoxic conditions is not as clear.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: Hif-1α and c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) are associated together in many tumor types.
source: Hif-1α and c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) are associated together in many tumor types (Comerford et al., 2004; Laderoute et al., 2004; An et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research showing association of Hif-1α and JNK in tumors.

claim: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) such as superoxide and peroxide radicals can cause both activation of the JNK pathway.
source: It is well established that reactive oxygen species (ROS) such as superoxide and peroxide radicals can cause both activation of the JNK pathway (Lo et al., 1996; Owusu-Ansah and Banerjee, 2009) and stabilization of Hif-1α (Dröge, 2002; Chandel et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on ROS effects.

claim: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) can cause stabilization of Hif-1α.
source: It is well established that reactive oxygen species (ROS) such as superoxide and peroxide radicals can cause both activation of the JNK pathway (Lo et al., 1996; Owusu-Ansah and Banerjee, 2009) and stabilization of Hif-1α (Dröge, 2002; Chandel et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on ROS effects.

claim: Persistent activation of JNK signaling is involved in cancer development, progression and perhaps cellular transformation.
source: It is increasingly apparent that persistent activation of JNK signaling is involved in cancer development, progression and perhaps cellular transformation (Manning and Davis, 2003; Raitano et al., 1995; Smeal et al., 1991; Wagner and Nebreda, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on JNK in cancer.

claim: JNK could have an indirect role in attenuating oxidative phosphorylation by activating PDHK, thus blocking PDH function.
source: In addition to the above functions, it is likely that JNK could have an indirect role in attenuating oxidative phosphorylation by activating PDHK, thus blocking PDH function (Zhou et al., 2009, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on JNK and PDHK.

claim: LDH has been demonstrated to be a marker for poor prognosis in multiple malignancies such as renal cell carcinoma.
source: Importantly, LDH has been demonstrated to be a marker for poor prognosis in multiple malignancies such as renal cell carcinoma (Armstrong et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to clinical research on LDH as a prognostic marker.

claim: The Drosophila genome contains a single gene encoding an LDH enzyme (ImpL3).
source: The Drosophila genome contains a single gene encoding an LDH enzyme (ImpL3), and biochemical studies demonstrate that it functions most like LDHA, the human form predominantly expressed in skeletal muscle that favors the conversion of pyruvate to lactate (Rechsteiner, 1970).
evidence: This is supported by citation to biochemical characterization of Drosophila LDH.

claim: Drosophila LDH functions most like LDHA, the human form predominantly expressed in skeletal muscle that favors the conversion of pyruvate to lactate.
source: The Drosophila genome contains a single gene encoding an LDH enzyme (ImpL3), and biochemical studies demonstrate that it functions most like LDHA, the human form predominantly expressed in skeletal muscle that favors the conversion of pyruvate to lactate (Rechsteiner, 1970).
evidence: This is supported by citation to biochemical characterization.

claim: An increase in LDHA enzymatic activity has been observed in diverse malignant cancers.
source: An increase in LDHA enzymatic activity has been observed in diverse malignant cancers (Dang and Semenza, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research on LDHA in cancer.

claim: Endogenous LDH activity is not observed in epithelial imaginal tissues such as the wing and eye discs.
source: Endogenous LDH activity is not observed in epithelial imaginal tissues such as the wing and eye discs (Figure 1a; Figure 1—figure supplement 1a) that developmentally mature in the larva to give rise to the corresponding appendages in the adult (Swammerdam, 1737), although evidence for such endogenous expression can be observed in the brain and salivary glands (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c–d).
evidence: This is supported by enzymatic assay data shown in figures.

claim: Endogenous LDH expression can be observed in the brain and salivary glands.
source: Endogenous LDH activity is not observed in epithelial imaginal tissues such as the wing and eye discs (Figure 1a; Figure 1—figure supplement 1a) that developmentally mature in the larva to give rise to the corresponding appendages in the adult (Swammerdam, 1737), although evidence for such endogenous expression can be observed in the brain and salivary glands (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c–d).
evidence: This is supported by LDH-GFP expression data shown in figures.

claim: Activated PDGF/VEGF receptor (Pvr) causes robust LDH activity.
source: Using the Gal4/UAS system (Brand and Perrimon, 1993) to individually activate oncogenes in the wing disc, we found that the activated PDGF/VEGF receptor (known as Pvr) causes robust LDH activity (Figure 1b) while many other oncogenes do not (see later).
evidence: This is supported by enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Many other oncogenes do not cause robust LDH activity.
source: Using the Gal4/UAS system (Brand and Perrimon, 1993) to individually activate oncogenes in the wing disc, we found that the activated PDGF/VEGF receptor (known as Pvr) causes robust LDH activity (Figure 1b) while many other oncogenes do not (see later).
evidence: This is supported by data showing lack of LDH expression with other oncogenes in later figures.

claim: Activation of PDGF/VEGF Receptor leads to transcriptional up-regulation of LDH and the subsequent formation of active LDH enzyme in the tumor tissue.
source: Together, the enzyme and the reporter assay establish that activation of PDGF/VEGF Receptor leads to transcriptional up-regulation of LDH and the subsequent formation of active LDH enzyme in the tumor tissue.
evidence: This is supported by both enzymatic activity assays and LDH-GFP reporter expression data.

claim: Overexpression of the secreted ligand, Wingless causes overgrowth and duplication of the tissue but does not cause LDH expression.
source: For example, over-expression of the secreted ligand, Wingless (Neumann and Cohen, 1996), causes overgrowth and duplication of the tissue but does not cause LDH expression (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is supported by LDH-GFP expression data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Overexpression of the JAK/STAT pathway ligand Unpaired (Upd), promotes tissue growth but does not induce LDH expression.
source: Similarly, overexpression of the JAK/STAT pathway ligand Unpaired (Upd), promotes tissue growth (Chao et al., 2004; Rodrigues et al., 2012), but does not induce LDH expression (Figure 1g).
evidence: This is supported by LDH-GFP expression data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: The transcription factor Yorkie is a potent growth-promoting signal in the wing disc but at best, it induces very weak and variable expression of LDH-GFP in the wing pouch.
source: The transcription factor Yorkie is a potent growth-promoting signal in the wing disc (Huang et al., 2005), but at best, it induces very weak and variable expression of LDH-GFP in the wing pouch (Figure 1h).
evidence: This is supported by LDH-GFP expression data shown in Figure 1h.

claim: The up-regulation of LDH by Pvr is not a general consequence of stepped up cell proliferation seen in all tumors.
source: These results indicate that the up-regulation of LDH by Pvr is not a general consequence of stepped up cell proliferation seen in all tumors.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that other growth-promoting oncogenes do not induce LDH.

claim: Neither constitutively signaling form of the insulin receptor (InRact) nor the activated form of epidermal growth factor receptor (Egfract) can induce LDH-GFP expression even though both cause significant overgrowth of the tissue.
source: Furthermore, given Pvr's function as an RTK, it was initially a surprise to find that neither constitutively signaling form of the insulin receptor (InRact, Figure 1i) nor the activated form of epidermal growth factor receptor (Egfract; Figure 1j) can induce LDH-GFP expression even though both cause significant overgrowth of the tissue.
evidence: This is supported by LDH-GFP expression data shown in Figures 1i and 1j.

claim: The observed specificity of Pvr, compared with other RTKs, in the expression of LDH, presents a unique opportunity for investigating the mechanism by which an oncogene can regulate the metabolism of a tumor tissue.
source: This observed specificity of Pvr, compared with other RTKs, in the expression of LDH, presents a unique opportunity for investigating the mechanism by which an oncogene can regulate the metabolism of a tumor tissue.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the findings for future research.

claim: Drosophila Hifα (called Sima) is rapidly degraded under normoxic conditions and therefore no Sima protein is detected in the wild-type wing disc.
source: As with the mammalian counterpart, Drosophila Hifα (called Sima) is rapidly degraded under normoxic conditions and therefore no Sima protein is detected in the wild-type wing disc (Figure 2a), but Sima protein is stabilized in a Pvract background (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Sima protein is stabilized in a Pvract background.
source: As with the mammalian counterpart, Drosophila Hifα (called Sima) is rapidly degraded under normoxic conditions and therefore no Sima protein is detected in the wild-type wing disc (Figure 2a), but Sima protein is stabilized in a Pvract background (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Overexpression of Sima robustly induces both LDH activity and expression.
source: Overexpression of Sima (but not of a Sima mutant lacking its DNA binding domain) robustly induces both LDH activity and expression (Figure 2c–d; Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by LDH activity and LDH-GFP expression data shown in the figures.

claim: Overexpression of a Sima mutant lacking its DNA binding domain does not robustly induce LDH activity and expression.
source: Overexpression of Sima (but not of a Sima mutant lacking its DNA binding domain) robustly induces both LDH activity and expression (Figure 2c–d; Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by LDH-GFP expression data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Overexpression of Sima causes growth defects, similar to the phenotypes of the Hph mutant.
source: It also causes growth defects, similar to the phenotypes of the Hph mutant (Centanin et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research on Hph mutant phenotypes.

claim: LDH expression induced by Pvract is strongly suppressed upon silencing sima using either one of two independent transgenic RNAi constructs.
source: Importantly, LDH expression induced by Pvract is strongly suppressed upon silencing sima using either one of two independent transgenic RNAi constructs (Figure 2e–f).
evidence: This is supported by LDH-GFP expression data shown in Figures 2e and 2f.

claim: Sima is essential for LDH induction by Pvract.
source: Thus, Sima is essential for LDH induction by Pvract.
evidence: This is concluded from the RNAi suppression experiments.

claim: Knockdown of sima suppresses some of the overgrowth caused by Pvract, but this effect is small (about a 20% reduction in volume).
source: Knockdown of sima does suppress some of the overgrowth caused by Pvract, but this effect is small (about a 20% reduction in volume. see Figure 2—figure supplement 1b) and the tumor-growth loss is clearly not as robust as the complete loss of LDH-GFP seen using the same knockdown construct.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative volume measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Tumor growth is a result of multiple interacting events, and blocking glycolysis alone will not be sufficient to fully rescue the growth of a tumor.
source: We conclude that tumor growth is a result of multiple interacting events, and blocking glycolysis alone will not be sufficient to fully rescue the growth of a tumor.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that sima knockdown only partially suppresses tumor growth.

claim: One mechanism for Sima stabilization could involve the hypoxic environment that might exist within the disorganized mass of a tumor tissue.
source: The Pvr induced tumor is characterized by unrestrained, disorganized growth, and in principle, one mechanism for Sima stabilization could involve the hypoxic environment that might exist within the disorganized mass of a tumor tissue.
evidence: This is a hypothesis considered by the authors.

claim: Examples of a mechanism in which deeper tissues within solid tumors become hypoxic have been demonstrated in human cancers.
source: Examples of such a mechanism in which deeper tissues within solid tumors become hypoxic have been demonstrated in human cancers (Bertout et al., 2008; Keith and Simon, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on tumor hypoxia.

claim: In addition to hypoxia, Hif can be stabilized under normoxic conditions by multiple metabolites such as NO, ROS, succinate, and fumarate.
source: However, it is also true that in addition to hypoxia, Hif can be stabilized under normoxic conditions by multiple metabolites such as NO, ROS, succinate, and fumarate (Chandel et al., 2000; Isaacs et al., 2005; Selak et al., 2005; Mateo et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on Hif stabilization mechanisms.

claim: Single or small groups of cells expressing Pvract that are surrounded by normal tissue express LDH in a strikingly cell-autonomous fashion.
source: To address whether the Pvr induced LDH-GFP expression is specifically due to a hypoxic core within a tumor, we utilized the AyGal4 system (Ito et al., 1997) to generate flip-out clones expressing Pvract. This technique allows analysis of LDH expression in single or small groups of cells expressing Pvract that are surrounded by normal tissue. Under these conditions, there is no over-growth or tumor formation, yet these single/small number cell clones express LDH in a strikingly cell-autonomous fashion (Figure 2g).
evidence: This is supported by LDH-GFP expression data in clones shown in Figure 2g.

claim: A large tumor with a hypoxic core is not a requirement for Sima stabilization or LDH expression.
source: We conclude that a large tumor with a hypoxic core is not a requirement for Sima stabilization or LDH expression.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that single cells expressing Pvract show LDH expression.

claim: Ras is the major effector of RTK signaling.
source: Ras is the major effector of RTK signaling (Moodie et al., 1993; Vivanco and Sawyers, 2002), and indeed we have found that constitutively active dRas1 is sufficient for a small increase in LDH expression and activity (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on Ras function.

claim: Constitutively active dRas1 is sufficient for a small increase in LDH expression and activity.
source: Ras is the major effector of RTK signaling (Moodie et al., 1993; Vivanco and Sawyers, 2002), and indeed we have found that constitutively active dRas1 is sufficient for a small increase in LDH expression and activity (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is supported by LDH-GFP expression data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Induction of LDH by Pvract is suppressed by a dominant-negative mutant allele of Ras (dRas1N17).
source: Also, induction of LDH by Pvract is suppressed by a dominant-negative mutant allele of Ras (dRas1N17) (Lee et al., 1996) (Figure 3h).
evidence: This is supported by LDH-GFP expression data shown in Figure 3h.

claim: Egfract causes phosphorylation of ERK but not AKT.
source: We found that Egfract causes phosphorylation of ERK but not AKT (Figure 3a,d), while InRact activates Akt but not ERK (Figure 3b,e).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 3a and 3d.

claim: InRact activates Akt but not ERK.
source: We found that Egfract causes phosphorylation of ERK but not AKT (Figure 3a,d), while InRact activates Akt but not ERK (Figure 3b,e).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 3b and 3e.

claim: Pvract induces both ERK and PI3K/Akt pathways.
source: In this system, Pvract induces both pathways (Figure 3c,f) and thus we tested the function of each pathway and then both in combination in the control of LDH expression.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 3c and 3f.

claim: RNAi initiated knock down of Dsor1 (MAPKK) or ERK (Rl, rolled), potently suppresses LDH-GFP induction downstream of Pvract.
source: RNAi initiated knock down of Dsor1 (MAPKK) or ERK (Rl, rolled), potently suppresses LDH-GFP induction downstream of Pvract (Figure 3i–j).
evidence: This is supported by LDH-GFP expression data shown in Figures 3i and 3j.

claim: ERK pathway is essential for Pvr-mediated LDH upregulation.
source: Thus, ERK pathway is essential for Pvr-mediated LDH upregulation.
evidence: This is concluded from the RNAi suppression experiments.

claim: LDH-GFP expression is suppressed upon loss of PI3K pathway members including PI3K, Akt, or TOR.
source: Similarly, when we blocked PI3K signaling in a Pvract background using several independent ways, including co-expression of an RNAi against PI3K (Figure 3k), a dominant-negative mutant form of PI3K (Figure 3l), inactivation of Akt by RNAi (Figure 3m), or silencing dTOR by RNAi (Figure 3n), each combination suppresses the induction of LDH-GFP.
evidence: This is supported by LDH-GFP expression data shown in Figures 3k-n.

claim: Pvract dependent accumulation of Sima protein is significantly suppressed when either Dsor1 or Akt is silenced.
source: Finally, Pvract dependent accumulation of Sima protein is significantly suppressed when either Dsor1 or Akt is silenced (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–b).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a-b.

claim: The PI3K/Akt/TOR axis is definitively needed for LDH regulation.
source: Thus, the PI3K/Akt/TOR axis is also definitively needed for LDH regulation.
evidence: This is concluded from the multiple suppression experiments targeting this pathway.

claim: Individual overexpression of either an activated form of human Raf (hRafact) or a constitutively active form of PI3K (PI3Kact) does not induce LDH-GFP expression although each genotype causes significant over-growth.
source: Importantly, individual overexpression of either an activated form of human Raf (hRafact) or a constitutively active form of PI3K (PI3Kact, active due to a mutation in the p110α catalytic subunit) (Brand and Perrimon, 1994; Leevers et al., 1996) does not induce LDH-GFP expression although each genotype causes significant over-growth (Figure 3o–p).
evidence: This is supported by LDH-GFP expression data shown in Figures 3o and 3p.

claim: Co-expression of hRafact and PI3Kact leads to extensive LDH induction even more robustly than what is seen for Pvract.
source: In combination, however, co-expression of hRafact and PI3Kact either using drivers or in small clones, leads to extensive LDH induction even more robustly than what is seen for Pvract (Figure 3q–r).
evidence: This is supported by LDH-GFP expression data shown in Figures 3q and 3r.

claim: Dual PI3K/ERK activation is sufficient to increase Sima expression.
source: Furthermore, dual PI3K/ERK activation is also sufficient to increase Sima expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c–d).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c-d.

claim: Knock down of Sima significantly attenuates PI3K/ERK induced LDH-GFP expression.
source: Knock down of Sima significantly attenuates PI3K/ERK induced LDH-GFP expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1h–i).
evidence: This is supported by LDH-GFP expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1h-i.

claim: Sima is the critical regulator of glycolytic genes upon co-activating PI3K and ERK pathways.
source: Similar to its role in mediating Pvract induced LDH expression, this demonstrates that Sima is the critical regulator of glycolytic genes upon co-activating PI3K and ERK pathways.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that Sima knockdown suppresses LDH expression induced by PI3K/ERK co-activation.

claim: A combination of ERK and PI3K signaling is both necessary and sufficient to induce Hifα-dependent LDH induction.
source: We conclude that a combination of ERK and PI3K signaling is both necessary and sufficient to induce Hifα-dependent LDH induction.
evidence: This is concluded from the genetic epistasis experiments showing requirement and sufficiency.

claim: On its own, each signal (ERK or PI3K) is necessary but not sufficient to cause LDH expression.
source: On its own, each signal is necessary but not sufficient to cause LDH expression.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that individual pathway activation does not induce LDH but knockdown of either pathway suppresses Pvr-induced LDH.

claim: InR/TOR pathway is associated with translational control in diverse systems.
source: InR/TOR pathway is associated with translational control in diverse systems (Fukuda et al., 2002; Hay and Sonenberg, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on InR/TOR pathway function.

claim: Both translation and degradation critically control Hifα level.
source: In particular, both translation and degradation critically control Hifα level (Bacon et al., 1998; Gorr et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on Hifα regulation.

claim: The induction of LDH by Pvract/Sima remains unaffected when Pointed (Drosophila ETS2), the well–established direct nuclear target of the ERK pathway, is mutated.
source: Consistent with this notion, the induction of LDH by Pvract/Sima remains unaffected when Pointed (Drosophila ETS2), the well–established direct nuclear target of the ERK pathway (O'Neill et al., 1994), is mutated (Figure 3v).
evidence: This is supported by LDH-GFP expression data shown in Figure 3v.

claim: The ribosomal S6 kinase is a known target of TOR signaling that promotes translation of a subset of mRNA transcripts, including Hif-1α.
source: In contrast, the ribosomal S6 kinase, a known target of TOR signaling that promotes translation of a subset of mRNA transcripts, including Hif-1α (Ma and Blenis, 2009) is prominently involved in this process since a dominant-negative form of S6k is a strong suppressor of Pvr-mediated LDH induction and Sima accumulation (Figure 3s and Figure 3—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research on S6K function.

claim: A dominant-negative form of S6k is a strong suppressor of Pvr-mediated LDH induction and Sima accumulation.
source: In contrast, the ribosomal S6 kinase, a known target of TOR signaling that promotes translation of a subset of mRNA transcripts, including Hif-1α (Ma and Blenis, 2009) is prominently involved in this process since a dominant-negative form of S6k is a strong suppressor of Pvr-mediated LDH induction and Sima accumulation (Figure 3s and Figure 3—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: This is supported by LDH-GFP expression and Sima immunohistochemistry data shown in the figures.

claim: Lk6 binds ERK and phosphorylates the initiation factor eIF4E to promote Cap dependent translation.
source: The ERK signal also modulates protein translation through the Mnk kinase (LK6 in Drosophila). Lk6 binds ERK and phosphorylates the initiation factor eIF4E to promote Cap dependent translation (Arquier et al., 2005; Parra-Palau et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on Lk6/Mnk function.

claim: A single-copy loss of lk6 strongly suppresses LDH induction and Sima accumulation downstream of Pvr.
source: Strikingly, we find that a single-copy loss of lk6 strongly suppresses LDH induction and Sima accumulation downstream of Pvr (Figure 3t and Figure 3—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: This is supported by LDH-GFP expression and Sima immunohistochemistry data shown in the figures.

claim: 4E-BP (Thor) is a downstream effector of the PI3K/Akt pathway that forms a complex with elF4E and inhibits translation.
source: Finally, published literature (Miron et al., 2001) has established 4E-BP (Thor) as a downstream effector of the PI3K/Akt pathway that forms a complex with elF4E and inhibits translation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research on 4E-BP function.

claim: mTOR phosphorylates 4E-BP releasing it from eIF4E allowing efficient translation.
source: mTOR phosphorylates 4E-BP releasing it from eIF4E (Furic et al., 2010) allowing efficient translation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research on mTOR and 4E-BP.

claim: Co-expression of 4E-BP with Pvract suppresses LDH induction.
source: We found that co-expression of 4E-BP with Pvract suppresses LDH induction (Figure 3u).
evidence: This is supported by LDH-GFP expression data shown in Figure 3u.

claim: ERK and PI3K pathways converge at the level of translational control of gene products including Sima.
source: Taken together, these data strongly support a mechanism in which ERK and PI3K pathways converge at the level of translational control of gene products including Sima.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that translational regulators downstream of both pathways are required for Sima accumulation and LDH expression.

claim: Initially, the increased translation of sima transcript generates sufficient Sima protein (in excess of the rate of Sima degradation), leading to LDH induction.
source: We propose that initially, the increased translation of sima transcript generates sufficient Sima protein (in excess of the rate of Sima degradation), leading to LDH induction; later we will show that this reprogramming is further augmented by a feedback loop involving ROS.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the data showing translational control of Sima.

claim: RNA-Seq data confirms the transcriptional up-regulation of LDH in Pvract background.
source: Our results confirm the transcriptional up-regulation of LDH.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data comparing different genotypes.

claim: The transcription of six of the ten glycolytic enzymes is up-regulated in a Pvract background of which four –Hex-A, Pfk, Ald and Impl3- are regulated in a Sima dependent manner.
source: Interestingly, the transcription of six of the ten glycolytic enzymes is up-regulated in a Pvract background of which four –Hex-A, Pfk, Ald and Impl3- are regulated in a Sima dependent manner (Figure 4a–b).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4a-b.

claim: Hex-A (hexokinase-A) phosphorylates glucose to generate glucose 6-p in the first step of glycolysis.
source: Hex-A (hexokinase-A) phosphorylates glucose to generate glucose 6-p in the first step of glycolysis.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about hexokinase function.

claim: Pfk (phosphofructo kinase) phosphorylates fructose 1-p to generate fructose 1,6-bp.
source: Similarly, Pfk (phosphofructo kinase) phosphorylates fructose 1-p to generate fructose 1,6-bp, whereas Ald (Aldolase) converts fructose 1,6-bp to glyceraldehyde 3-p in the next step.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about phosphofructokinase function.

claim: Ald (Aldolase) converts fructose 1,6-bp to glyceraldehyde 3-p.
source: Similarly, Pfk (phosphofructo kinase) phosphorylates fructose 1-p to generate fructose 1,6-bp, whereas Ald (Aldolase) converts fructose 1,6-bp to glyceraldehyde 3-p in the next step.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about aldolase function.

claim: Impl3/LDH (lactate dehydrogenase) converts pyruvate to lactate in the final step of glycolysis.
source: Impl3/LDH (lactate dehydrogenase) converts pyruvate to lactate in the final step of glycolysis.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about LDH function.

claim: Pvr and Sima-dependent regulation of key glycolytic enzymes indicates a more efficient usage of the entire glycolytic pathway.
source: Pvr and Sima-dependent regulation of these key enzymes indicates a more efficient usage of the entire glycolytic pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that multiple rate-limiting glycolytic enzymes are upregulated.

claim: A subset of cancer cells attenuate mitochondrial respiration in addition to displaying increased aerobic glycolysis.
source: In addition to displaying increased aerobic glycolysis, a subset of cancer cells also attenuate mitochondrial respiration (Pelicano et al., 2006; Warburg, 1956a, 1956b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on cancer metabolism.

claim: The RNA-seq data identifies a set of transcripts encoding mitochondrial proteins that is down-regulated in Pvract background.
source: The RNA-seq data identifies a set of transcripts encoding mitochondrial proteins that is down-regulated in Pvract background.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Attenuation of ETC complex protein activity has been demonstrated to up-regulate transcripts for all glycolytic enzymes suggesting a cross talk between the two primary modes of metabolism.
source: Attenuation of ETC complex protein activity has also been demonstrated to up-regulate transcripts for all glycolytic enzymes suggesting a cross talk between the two primary modes of metabolism (Owusu-Ansah et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research on metabolic crosstalk.

claim: Pvract cells express PDHKtotal, active PDHK (phospho-PDHK), as well as the inactive form of PDH (p-PDH).
source: Just as LDH drives glycolysis by converting pyruvate to lactate, pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) drives the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation by converting pyruvate to acetyl-CoA. PDH is inactive when phosphorylated by p-PDHK. When stained with appropriate antibodies, Pvract cells are found to express PDHKtotal, active PDHK (phospho-PDHK), as well as the inactive form of PDH (p-PDH) (Figure 5a–f).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 5a-f.

claim: The high p-PDH level is suppressed by co-expressing PDHK-dsRNA establishing that PDHK is indeed required for inactivation of PDH in Pvract cells.
source: The high p-PDH level is suppressed by co-expressing PDHK-dsRNA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a) establishing that PDHK is indeed required for inactivation of PDH in Pvract cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Co-activation of ERK and PI3K pathways dramatically increases PDHKtotal expression, but this PDHK is inactive.
source: An antibody that recognizes both the active and the inactive forms of PDHK shows that co-expression of hRafact and PI3Kact results in dramatic up-regulation of PDHKtotal. Similar to the results obtained for Sima, the regulation of PDHK protein is also at a translational level (Figure 5k; Figure 5—figure supplement 1o,q). Interestingly, while the combined activation of PI3Kact and hRafact is sufficient for PDHK production, the protein thus produced is inactive and is not recognized by a phospho-specific, p-PDHK antibody (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in the figures.

claim: p-PDH (the inactive form of PDH) is not seen when hRafact and PI3Kact are co-expressed.
source: This is unlike in Pvract cells where both PDHKtotal and PDHKactive are seen (Figure 5d–e). Consistent with this observation, p-PDH (the inactive form of PDH) is also not seen when hRafact and PI3Kact are co-expressed (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b), and yet is readily detectable in a Pvract background (Figure 5f).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Additional proteins independent of ERK and PI3K pathways function downstream of Pvr and are necessary to activate PDHK and thus inhibit PDH and mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation.
source: These results establish that additional proteins independent of ERK and PI3K pathways function downstream of Pvr and are necessary to activate PDHK and thus inhibit PDH and mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ERK/PI3K co-activation produces inactive PDHK.

claim: Src42A functions in epidermal closure during both embryogenesis and metamorphosis by regulating JNK signaling.
source: Src42A, a Drosophila c-src proto-oncogene homolog, functions in epidermal closure during both embryogenesis and metamorphosis by regulating JNK signaling (Tateno et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research on Src42A function.

claim: Src42A controls tumor invasion and cell death by activating JNK.
source: It has also been found that Src42A controls tumor invasion and cell death by activating JNK (Ma et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research on Src42A in tumors.

claim: In mammalian cancer studies, Src mediates tumor cell metastasis and angiogenesis induced by VEGF.
source: In mammalian cancer studies, Src mediates tumor cell metastasis and angiogenesis induced by VEGF (Eliceiri et al., 1999; Weis et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on Src in mammalian cancer.

claim: Both Src42A and JNK are extensively phosphorylated in Pvract cells.
source: Using phospho-specific antibodies, we found that both Src42A and JNK are extensively phosphorylated in Pvract cells (Figure 5g–j).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 5g-j.

claim: Knockdown of Src42A suppresses phospho-JNK accumulation induced by Pvract.
source: Knockdown of Src42A suppresses phospho-JNK accumulation induced by Pvract (Figure 5o), whereas over-expression of a dominant negative form of JNK (BskDN) does not significantly reduce phospho-Src levels (Figure 5s) indicating that Src42A functions upstream of JNK.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5o.

claim: Over-expression of a dominant negative form of JNK (BskDN) does not significantly reduce phospho-Src levels indicating that Src42A functions upstream of JNK.
source: Knockdown of Src42A suppresses phospho-JNK accumulation induced by Pvract (Figure 5o), whereas over-expression of a dominant negative form of JNK (BskDN) does not significantly reduce phospho-Src levels (Figure 5s) indicating that Src42A functions upstream of JNK.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5s.

claim: Knockdown of Src42A, or over-expression of BskDN partially suppresses the phosphorylation level of PDHK induced by Pvract.
source: Knockdown of Src42A, or over-expression of BskDN partially suppresses the phosphorylation level of PDHK induced by Pvract (Figure 5l–m).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 5l-m.

claim: Co-expression of hRafact and PI3Kact is unable to increase p-PDHK levels.
source: As shown earlier, co-expression of hRafact and PI3Kact is unable to increase p-PDHK levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c), but the simultaneous activation of ERK, PI3K and JNK pathways by using hRafact, PI3Kact and active JNKK (hemipterous, hepact), clearly up-regulates PDHK activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1d), and the resulting effect on PDH is also dramatic.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The simultaneous activation of ERK, PI3K and JNK pathways clearly up-regulates PDHK activity.
source: As shown earlier, co-expression of hRafact and PI3Kact is unable to increase p-PDHK levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c), but the simultaneous activation of ERK, PI3K and JNK pathways by using hRafact, PI3Kact and active JNKK (hemipterous, hepact), clearly up-regulates PDHK activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1d), and the resulting effect on PDH is also dramatic.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1d.

claim: A dominant negative form of JNK (BskDN) or loss of JNKK (hemipterous, hepRNAi) suppresses the formation of p-PDH upon Pvr activation.
source: A dominant negative form of JNK (BskDN) or loss of JNKK (hemipterous, hepRNAi) suppresses the formation of p-PDH upon Pvr activation (Figure 5n; Figure 5—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in the figures.

claim: JNK is required for activation of p-PDHK and as a result, sufficient to inactivate PDH by causing its phosphorylation.
source: Thus JNK is required for activation of p-PDHK and as a result, sufficient to inactivate PDH by causing its phosphorylation.
evidence: This is concluded from the genetic experiments showing JNK requirement for PDHK activation and PDH inactivation.

claim: Dysfunction of PDH within the mitochondrion is invariably associated with increased production of ROS.
source: Although over-active PDH can promote reactive oxygen species (ROS) production during high mitochondrial flux (Kaplon et al., 2013), dysfunction of PDH within the mitochondrion is invariably associated with increased production of ROS (Glushakova et al., 2011; Ambrus et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on PDH and ROS.

claim: Pvract cells exhibit high ROS levels detected by direct staining with the DHE dye or as monitored by gstD-GFP expression.
source: Thus, Pvract cells exhibit high ROS levels detected by direct staining with the DHE dye (Figure 6a–b) or as monitored by gstD-GFP expression (Robinson et al., 2006) (Figure 6c–d) frequently used as a surrogate for ROS, marking cells under oxidative stress (Ohsawa et al., 2012; Sykiotis and Bohmann, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by DHE staining and gstD-GFP expression data shown in Figures 6a-d.

claim: ROS induction in Pvract cells is suppressed when PDHKRNAi is co-expressed.
source: This ROS induction is suppressed when PDHKRNAi is co-expressed (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by DHE staining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Co-expression of hRafact and PI3Kact does not cause ROS production unlike that seen for Pvract.
source: Co-expression of hRafact and PI3Kact does not cause ROS production unlike that seen for Pvract (Figure 6e; Figure 6—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by DHE staining and gstD-GFP expression data shown in the figures.

claim: Pvract induced ROS is effectively suppressed in a BskDN (JNK dominant negative) genetic background.
source: Instead, Pvract induced ROS is effectively suppressed in a BskDN (JNK dominant negative) genetic background (Figure 6f; Figure 6—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is supported by DHE staining and gstD-GFP expression data shown in the figures.

claim: Knockdown of hep (JNKK) or Src42A suppresses Pvract induced ROS.
source: Similar effects are seen upon knockdown of hep (JNKK) or Src42A (Figure 6—figure supplement 1d–e).
evidence: This is supported by DHE staining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1d-e.

claim: Src-JNK signaling plays an important role in the inhibition of mitochondrial activity and in raising ROS levels in Pvract tumors.
source: Thus Src-JNK signaling plays an important role in the inhibition of mitochondrial activity and in raising ROS levels in Pvract tumors.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that blocking Src-JNK signaling suppresses ROS production.

claim: ROS can activate the JNK pathway through interaction with the upstream component ASK (JNKKK).
source: Two notable facts about ROS have a bearing on the data presented here. The first is that ROS can activate the JNK pathway through interaction with the upstream component ASK (JNKKK) (Tobiume et al., 2001; Owusu-Ansah and Banerjee, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on ROS and JNK activation.

claim: High ROS conditions result in potent stabilization of the Hif protein even under normoxic conditions.
source: The second is that high ROS conditions result in potent stabilization of the Hif protein even under normoxic conditions (Chandel et al., 2000; Fandrey et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on ROS and Hif stabilization.

claim: ROS generated downstream of both Hif and JNK can feedback and reinforce these two pathways.
source: This provides the opportunity for ROS generated downstream of both Hif and JNK, to feedback and reinforce these two pathways.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on known ROS effects on Hif and JNK.

claim: Expression of Peroxidasin (Pxn) shows the strongest ROS scavenging activity among several antioxidant proteins tested.
source: To test this hypothesis, several antioxidant (free radical scavenging) proteins were expressed to reduce the level of ROS. Of these, the strongest ROS scavenging activity was seen upon Peroxidasin (Pxn) expression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental testing of multiple antioxidant proteins.

claim: Co-expression of Pxn in Pvract discs decreases ROS and prevents JNK activation.
source: In addition to a decrease in ROS (Figure 6g–h), we found that JNK is no longer activated when Pxn is co-expressed in Pvract discs (Figure 6i–j).
evidence: This is supported by DHE staining and phospho-JNK immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 6g-j.

claim: LDH-GFP expression and the accumulation of Sima protein are strongly suppressed by co-expression of Pxn.
source: Similarly, LDH-GFP expression (Figure 6k–l) and the accumulation of Sima protein are strongly suppressed by co-expression of Pxn (Figure 6m–n).
evidence: This is supported by LDH-GFP expression and Sima immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 6k-n.

claim: ROS is the central player in enforcing the metabolic reprogramming.
source: These results establish ROS as the central player in enforcing the metabolic reprogramming.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that ROS scavenging suppresses multiple aspects of metabolic reprogramming.

claim: The shift to glycolysis is reinforced when ROS is generated as a subsequent step after initial establishment through activation of three oncogenic pathways by Pvr.
source: Initially established through the activation of three oncogenic pathways by Pvr, the shift to glycolysis is then reinforced when ROS is generated as a subsequent step.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the genetic epistasis and ROS scavenging experiments.

claim: ROS establishes one means to maintain a stable Warburg effect by oncogene activation.
source: This establishes one means to maintain a stable Warburg effect by oncogene activation.
evidence: This is concluded from the demonstration of ROS feedback reinforcing metabolic reprogramming.

claim: The three critical components involved in metabolic reprogramming are the two pyruvate-metabolism enzymes, LDH and PDH and the free radical metabolite class designated as ROS.
source: Although the details may seem to vary, the three critical components involved in this process are the two pyruvate-metabolism enzymes, LDH and PDH and the free radical metabolite class designated as ROS.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the findings of the study.

claim: During the acquisition of aerobic glycolytic activity in a tumor environment, LDH actively converts pyruvate to lactate, and high PDHK inactivates PDH resulting in low pyruvate to acetyl-CoA conversion, low TCA flux and electron transport activity.
source: During the acquisition of the aerobic glycolytic activity in a tumor environment, LDH actively converts pyruvate to lactate, and high PDHK inactivates PDH resulting in low pyruvate to acetyl-CoA conversion, low TCA flux and electron transport activity.
evidence: This is a summary of the metabolic changes observed in the study.

claim: These metabolic events can be sustained over long periods of tumor growth only when coupled with a feed back signal from accumulating ROS in a mechanism that reinforces and enhances the high-LDH/low-PDH activity state.
source: Our results suggest that these events can be sustained over long periods of tumor growth only when coupled with a feed back signal from accumulating ROS in a mechanism that reinforces and enhances the high-LDH/low-PDH activity state.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the ROS feedback data.

claim: This genetic study was achieved in an in vivo context of an animal that is only mutant for the one specific activated oncogene that is introduced and is otherwise normal.
source: This genetic study was achieved in an in vivo context of an animal that is only mutant for the one specific activated oncogene that we introduce and is otherwise normal.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: While hypoxic conditions might favor a glycolytic activation in general, hypoxia is not an essential component for a tumor to become glycolytic, as in this system, where Hif is stabilized by alternative means in a normoxic environment.
source: Also, while hypoxic conditions might favor a glycolytic activation in general, hypoxia is not an essential component for a tumor to become glycolytic, as in this system, where Hif is stabilized by alternative means in a normoxic environment.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that single cells expressing Pvract show metabolic reprogramming without hypoxia.

claim: Pvract triggers two parallel pathways in a Ras dependent manner: the PI3K/Akt pathway that targets the S6K protein and the Raf/ERK pathway targeting the L6K protein.
source: Pvract triggers two parallel pathways in a Ras dependent manner. The first is the PI3K/Akt pathway that targets the S6K protein important for translational initiation. The second is the Raf/ERK pathway targeting the L6K (MNK in mammals) protein that is also independently required for translational initiation.
evidence: This is a summary of the pathway analysis presented in the study.

claim: Both PI3K/Akt and Raf/ERK pathways must act simultaneously in order to establish translational control of both Hifα (Sima), and PDHK.
source: On their own, any one of these pathways can cause tumor growth, presumably due to independent downstream transcriptional events. But both pathways must act simultaneously in order to establish translational control of both Hifα (Sima), and PDHK.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that individual pathway activation is insufficient for Sima and PDHK upregulation.

claim: While the PI3K and ERK pathways acting together cause significant amounts of PDHK translation, the protein thus produced is inactive.
source: Interestingly, while the PI3K and ERK pathways acting together causes significant amounts of PDHK translation, the protein thus produced is inactive.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing PDHK protein but not phospho-PDHK.

claim: The PDHK translated in a Pvract background is enzymatically active and capable of inactivating PDH.
source: In contrast, the PDHK translated in a Pvract background is enzymatically active and capable of inactivating PDH.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing both PDHK and phospho-PDHK in Pvract cells.

claim: A pathway initiated by Pvract that involves Src and JNK helps generate the active form of PDHK.
source: Our data show that yet another parallel pathway initiated by Pvract that involves Src and JNK helps generate the active form of PDHK.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that Src/JNK are required for PDHK activation.

claim: All three downstream effectors of activated Pvr (Src/JNK, PI3K/S6K and ERK/Lk6, eIF4E) are essential in generating an active form of PDHK protein to down-regulate oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Therefore all three downstream effectors of activated Pvr (Src/JNK, PI3K/S6K and ERK/Lk6, eIF4E) are essential in generating an active form of PDHK protein to down-regulate oxidative phosphorylation, while only the last two of these pathways are needed for LDH production and glycolysis.
evidence: This is a summary of the pathway requirements determined by genetic analysis.

claim: Only PI3K/S6K and ERK/Lk6, eIF4E pathways are needed for LDH production and glycolysis.
source: Therefore all three downstream effectors of activated Pvr (Src/JNK, PI3K/S6K and ERK/Lk6, eIF4E) are essential in generating an active form of PDHK protein to down-regulate oxidative phosphorylation, while only the last two of these pathways are needed for LDH production and glycolysis.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that ERK/PI3K co-activation is sufficient for LDH expression.

claim: In the context of the triggering oncogene, the tumor caused could either be non-glycolytic, or be glycolytic but not lacking in oxidative phosphorylation.
source: It is easy to visualize how, in the context of the triggering oncogene, the tumor caused could either be non-glycolytic, or be glycolytic but not lacking in oxidative phosphorylation (Pavlova and Thompson, 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that different oncogenes activate different combinations of pathways.

claim: Direct pyruvate to acetyl-CoA conversion within the mitochondrion, and therefore the TCA flux will be attenuated since PDH function is inhibited by PDHK in the tumor cells.
source: In the system described in this paper, it is Inevitable that direct pyruvate to acetyl-CoA conversion within the mitochondrion, and therefore the TCA flux will be attenuated since PDH function is inhibited by PDHK in the tumor cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that PDHK is active and PDH is inactive in Pvract tumors.

claim: The level of ROS rises as the mitochondrion becomes dysfunctional.
source: While this sequence of events can initiate a switch in the metabolic profile of the cell, an additional mechanism is required to sustain this transition over a long period of time. The central player in this sustenance is ROS. The level of these free-radical species rises as the mitochondrion becomes dysfunctional (Sun et al., 2009; Glushakova et al., 2011; Owusu-Ansah et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on mitochondrial dysfunction and ROS.

claim: Excess ROS stabilizes Hif using the same mechanism that is used during hypoxia, thus reinforcing the glycolytic pathways.
source: Importantly, this excess ROS functions as a feedback signal that has at least two important consequences. First, ROS stabilizes Hif using the same mechanism that is used during hypoxia (Chandel et al., 2000; Fandrey et al., 2006), thus reinforcing the glycolytic pathways.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on ROS and Hif stabilization.

claim: ROS can activate the JNK pathway, and after the initial reprogramming in metabolism, the transition is made stable over time, as the generated ROS reinforces the upstream members.
source: The second is that ROS can activate the JNK pathway (Tobiume et al., 2001; Owusu-Ansah and Banerjee, 2009). Thus, after the initial reprogramming in metabolism, the transition is made stable over time, as the generated ROS reinforces the upstream members.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on known ROS effects and the experimental data.

claim: Scavenging ROS blocks phosphorylation of components that are upstream of it.
source: All of the results shown here are consistent with this positive feedback model that enforces the Warburg effect and sustains it over time. For example, scavenging ROS blocks phosphorylation of components that are upstream of it (Figure 6i–j).
evidence: This is supported by data showing that Pxn expression suppresses JNK phosphorylation.

claim: Activation of PI3K and Raf together does not raise ROS even as it increases LDH.
source: Unlike Pvr, activation of PI3K and Raf together does not raise ROS even as it increases LDH (Figure 3q and Figure 6e); and activation of Ras, which will not lead to high ROS causes only very weak metabolic reprogramming compared with Pvract (Figure 1d–e).
evidence: This is supported by ROS and LDH expression data shown in the figures.

claim: Activation of Ras causes only very weak metabolic reprogramming compared with Pvract.
source: Unlike Pvr, activation of PI3K and Raf together does not raise ROS even as it increases LDH (Figure 3q and Figure 6e); and activation of Ras, which will not lead to high ROS causes only very weak metabolic reprogramming compared with Pvract (Figure 1d–e).
evidence: This is supported by LDH expression data shown in the figures.

claim: The positive feedback function of ROS is a critical step in tumors undergoing metabolic reprogramming or cell lines that are not necessarily under hypoxic conditions.
source: Thus, the positive feedback function of ROS is a critical step in tumors undergoing metabolic reprogramming or cell lines that are not necessarily under hypoxic conditions.
evidence: This is concluded from the demonstration that ROS feedback is essential for maintaining metabolic reprogramming.

claim: Tissue hypoxia stabilizes Hif and would be true of large non-vascularized solid tumors but not necessarily in circulating cells or in cancer cell lines.
source: Although tissue hypoxia does stabilize Hif (Wenger, 2002), this would be true of large non-vascularized solid tumors but not necessarily in circulating cells or in cancer cell lines.
evidence: This is a statement about the context-dependence of hypoxia-mediated Hif stabilization.

claim: The mechanism detailed in the model is Hif dependent but hypoxia independent, a condition often observed in human cancers.
source: The mechanism detailed in Figure 7 is Hif dependent but hypoxia independent, a condition often observed in human cancers (Lee et al., 2008; Ivan et al., 2001; Zhong et al., 2000; Park et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on hypoxia-independent Hif stabilization in human cancers.

claim: Transcript levels of PDHK or Sima are not altered in Pvract cells, whereas the PDHK and Sima protein levels are very significantly up-regulated by Pvract through the translational module controlled by PI3K/ERK pathways.
source: Consistent with translational control, transcript levels of PDHK or Sima are not altered in Pvract cells, whereas the PDHK and Sima protein levels are very significantly up-regulated by Pvract through the translational module controlled by PI3K/ERK pathways.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and qRT-PCR data showing no change in transcript levels, and immunohistochemistry showing increased protein levels.

claim: Unlike in several published mammalian studies, there is no evidence for transcriptional control of PDHK by Hif in this Drosophila system.
source: Unlike in several published mammalian studies (Kaplon et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2006), we did not find evidence for transcriptional control of PDHK by Hif.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and qRT-PCR data showing no change in PDHK transcript levels.

claim: Analysis of RNA-Seq data reveals that PDHK transcription levels remain unaltered in Pvract background.
source: Analysis of our RNA-Seq data reveals that PDHK transcription levels remain unaltered in Pvract background (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The activation of a single oncogene, the PDGF/VEGF Receptor (Pvr) induces multiple phenotypes associated with tumor formation, including overgrowth, cell shape change, local migration and a likely shift in metabolism from oxidative phosphorylation to aerobic glycolysis.
source: It is interesting that the activation of a single oncogene, the PDGF/VEGF Receptor (Pvr) induces multiple phenotypes associated with tumor formation, including overgrowth, cell shape change, local migration and importantly for this study, a likely shift in metabolism from oxidative phosphorylation to aerobic glycolysis.
evidence: This is a summary of the phenotypes observed upon Pvr activation.

claim: These tumors are not metastatic presumably because this requires complete loss of epithelial polarity.
source: These tumors are not metastatic presumably because this requires complete loss of epithelial polarity (Pagliarini and Xu, 2003; Wu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from published research on requirements for metastasis.

claim: Although only a single oncogene is activated, the observed Warburg effect is caused by the activation of several interconnected pathways that are precisely dissected in this genetically tractable model system.
source: Although only a single oncogene is activated, the observed Warburg effect is caused by the activation of several interconnected pathways that are precisely dissected in this genetically tractable model system.
evidence: This is a summary of the approach and findings of the study.

claim: The distinct advantage of this analysis is that the tumor is generated in an otherwise wild-type background such that the pathways activated reflect primary drivers of the different aspects of the tumor and the analysis is not complicated by background mutations.
source: The distinct advantage of this analysis is that the tumor is generated in an otherwise wild-type background such that the pathways activated reflect primary drivers of the different aspects of the tumor and the analysis is not complicated by background mutations.
evidence: This describes the advantage of the Drosophila genetic approach used in the study.

claim: In some cancer cell-lines, a Warburg effect is often entirely attributed to PI3K activation, but this interpretation is complicated by the presence of background mutations that make cell-lines immortal.
source: In some cancer cell-lines, a Warburg effect is often entirely attributed to PI3K activation (DeBerardinis et al., 2008). This interpretation is complicated by the presence of background mutations that make cell-lines immortal, before they are transformed.
evidence: This is a critique of cell line studies supported by citation and general knowledge.

claim: PI3K activated tumors are often seen only in backgrounds in which either Raf, ERK or Ras is activated.
source: For example, PI3K activated tumors are often seen only in backgrounds in which either Raf, ERK or Ras is activated (McCubrey et al., 2007; Steelman et al., 2008; Yuan and Cantley, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on PI3K and other pathway interactions.

claim: Given the complete conservation of all the relevant components between Drosophila and mammals, it is reasonable to propose that a similar set of epistatic relationships to the one proposed here, will hold in mammalian cancers.
source: Given the complete conservation of all the relevant components between Drosophila and mammals, it is reasonable to propose that a similar set of epistatic relationships to the one proposed here, will hold in mammalian cancers.
evidence: This is a speculation about the applicability of the findings to mammalian systems based on conservation of components.
